claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin iron-oxide film under ambient conditions.
The native iron-oxide layer on Q235 steel is locally protective at room temperature.
At room temperature, the native oxide acts as a continuous barrier that slows corrosion.
Exposure to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C causes fluxing of the oxide scale on Q235 steel.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide scale and Q235 substrate contributes to high-temperature scale degradation.
Salt-induced fluxing and thermal mismatch cause microcracking or spallation of the oxide scale.
Microcracking or spallation exposes the underlying steel and accelerates corrosion.
In the absence of salt, including at high temperature, the oxide scale remains coherent and limits degradation.
Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C will show greater mass change than room-temperature controls or high-temperature controls without salt.
Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C will show more extensive oxide-scale degradation than the controls.
The high-temperature salt-exposed samples will retain less corrosion protection than the controls.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to low-alloy steels such as Q235 that rely on a native oxide layer for protection.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to stainless or boiler steels that form thicker or more chemically robust protective scales.
A sodium-sulfate-based salt is an example of an aggressive salt suitable for testing the proposed mechanism.
The governing mediator is the continuity and integrity of the native iron-oxide scale across the Q235 surface.
